description: Coordinate three independently running workers so their work completes in role order 0, 1, 2, regardless of thread launch or scheduling order. Implement RunOrdered(role,context), called once by each worker with its role. Call that worker context.Work() exactly once. Work for role 1 must not begin until role 0 work finishes; role 2 must wait for role 1 work to finish. Returning or sorting a list does not perform the work.
constraints: The judge starts three real threads (Node worker_threads for JavaScript), each calling the same implementation independently with role 0, 1 or 2. Each worker receives its own wrapper around one shared SyncContext state. Use only the provided context API for coordination and work. Return void/None/undefined. Do not launch extra threads or use sleeps, delays or polling as a substitute for synchronization.

context.Wait(gate) atomically consumes a permit from gate 0 or 1, blocking until one exists. context.Signal(gate) adds one permit and wakes a waiter. Both counting-semaphore gates start with zero permits and belong to this one case. Calls on an invalid gate, more than 20 total Wait/Signal/Work calls per worker or a context from another worker fail the case. Wait/Signal are thread-safe; caller work is not automatically ordered.

context.Work() invokes opaque actual work owned by that worker; it may take time before returning. It must execute exactly once in each worker, and no dependent worker may begin its Work until its predecessor Work returns. Primitive calls may synchronize the workers but must not run another role work on their behalf. Contexts are opaque supplied objects; their fields/underlying shared storage must not be inspected or altered.

JSON launchOrder is a permutation of [0,1,2]; delayMask is a test scheduling input in 0..3; the context wire placeholder is []. These are private judge inputs, not the callable parameters: the callable receives role and its provided context. The judge varies launch order and independent entry delays without revealing a required sleep duration. A bounded execution timeout rejects noncompletion; passing sampled schedules alone is not a proof for every scheduler.

The displayed result is a private completion-order observation [0,1,2], never a return value to construct. Instances have independent gates and work state. No fairness bound or real-time latency guarantee is required; assume runnable threads are eventually scheduled.
why: Create one synchronization edge after each predecessor finishes its Work. Role 0 signals gate 0 only after returning from Work; role 1 must consume that permit before entering Work, then signals gate 1 afterward. Role 2 consumes gate 1 before entering Work. Semaphore permits persist when a signal happens before the corresponding wait, so neither launch order nor a guessed delay matters.
correctness: Gate 0 initially has no permit and only role 0 signals it, after its Work returns. Therefore role 1 cannot pass its Wait until role 0 completes. Similarly gate 1 is signaled only after role 1 Work returns, so role 2 starts only after role 1 completes. Each worker calls Work exactly once and each required signal/wait occurs once. There is no wait in role 0, so it eventually finishes and enables role 1, which eventually enables role 2 under eventual scheduling. Signals before waits remain available and do not create lost wakeups. Both required completion dependencies and termination follow without relying on timing.
walkthrough: Suppose workers start in order [2,1,0]. Role 2 blocks on gate 1; role 1 blocks on gate 0. Role 0 performs its Work and then signals gate 0. Role 1 consumes that permit, performs its Work and signals gate 1. Role 2 now performs its Work. If role 0 instead finishes before role 1 starts, gate 0 retains its permit and the same order follows.
time: O(1) synchronization operations per worker and O(W0+W1+W2) required sequential work duration, excluding unbounded scheduler waiting; no spin loop is used.
space: O(1) shared semaphore state and O(1) local storage per worker, excluding the judge worker stacks and opaque work.
edges: All six thread launch orders, signals before waits and predecessor entry delays.
Work completion rather than only start order; guessed sleeps are insufficient.
Repeated independent cases must not reuse stale permits or static work state.
Missing work, duplicate work, wrong gate and deadlock must fail.
related: The public Foo implementation establishes first/second/third work ordering through two semaphores. This callable supplies those two initially empty gates and private work callbacks so the grader can execute native workers and observe completion dependencies in every supported language.

languageWhy.java: Java calls the supplied context from three real Thread instances. Semaphore acquisition supplies the dependency before Work and release follows completion; no Thread.sleep assumption appears in the submitted method.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ receives SyncContext by reference, borrowing judge-owned shared coordination state. Wait/Signal block and signal native condition-variable semaphore permits; the method owns no thread or context lifetime.

description: Coordinate four independently running FizzBuzz workers to print exactly the values for 1 through limit, in increasing numeric order. Role 0 prints ordinary numbers, role 1 prints Fizz for multiples of 3 only, role 2 prints Buzz for multiples of 5 only, and role 3 prints FizzBuzz for multiples of both. Implement RunFizzBuzz(role,limit,context), called once by each actual worker. Use context.Print(value) for that worker assigned items; do not return an output array or run every role from one worker.
constraints: limit is 0..100. Four real native threads (Node worker_threads in JavaScript) call the implementation with distinct roles 0..3, sharing a supplied FizzContext coordination state. Each call returns void/None/undefined. The judge chooses launch order and independent entry delays. Assume eventually scheduled runnable workers, not a particular order or maximum scheduling latency.

context.Wait(gate) consumes one counting-semaphore permit from gate 0..3, blocking if empty; Signal(gate) adds one permit. Initially only gate 0 has one permit, all other gates have zero. Gates belong to this case, never previous cases. Use only these supplied primitives and Print for coordination; no extra threads, sleeps or polling. Each worker may make at most 4*(limit+1) total API calls; invalid gates and foreign-worker contexts fail.

context.Print(value) performs the current worker actual output work and may take time before returning. It accepts only the next integer in 1..limit and only from the assigned role: both-divisible first, then only-3, only-5 or ordinary-number role. Calls must not overlap or duplicate an item. It emits the corresponding Fizz/Buzz/FizzBuzz token or invariant decimal number; its output is observed privately, not built by your return value.

A JSON fixture contains limit, a permutation launchOrder of [0,1,2,3], scheduling delayMask in 0..15, and [] for the context. These are private scheduling inputs; the callable receives role, limit and an opaque context, not a launch-order array. Do not inspect context internals or underlying shared memory. Contexts and permits are isolated across cases.

Displayed output is the private printed-token transcript. For limit=0, no worker prints and all four return. Every value 1..limit must be printed exactly once in order, including limit when it is divisible by 3, 5 or both. A bounded runtime timeout rejects noncompletion; sampled schedules supplement the synchronization proof, not a universal scheduler guarantee.
why: The roles can determine their own values from divisibility; only the order between roles needs coordination. Keep one permit as a baton for the next value. A worker waits on its role gate before printing its value, then signals the role responsible for the next integer after printing finishes. Consecutive ordinary numbers can pass the baton back to the same gate, whose permit persists until the next wait.
correctness: Initially value 1 belongs to ordinary role 0, which alone has a permit. Assume exactly values 1 through v-1 have completed and the sole permit belongs to the role for v. Other roles wait without printing. The owner eventually consumes its permit, prints v from its own worker, and only after Print returns signals the owner of v+1 when one exists. This preserves increasing, nonoverlapping, exactly-once output and the baton invariant. Each role scans values increasingly, so it reaches each of its required waits in order and cannot skip an owned item. The final value needs no successor signal, and all remaining role iterations perform no work; all workers return. For limit=0 all loops are empty. Both-divisible ownership is tested first, preventing duplicate Fizz/Buzz output at multiples of 15.
walkthrough: For limit 5, role 0 consumes its initial permit and prints 1, then signals gate 0 for 2. After printing 2 it signals gate 1, so the Fizz worker prints value 3 as Fizz. That worker signals gate 0 for 4; after 4, role 0 signals gate 2 so Buzz prints value 5. No successor signal is needed. The private transcript is ["1","2","Fizz","4","Buzz"], regardless of worker launch order.
time: O(limit) total scanning work across four fixed workers and O(limit) synchronization/output calls. Required output work is sequential by specification; elapsed time also includes unbounded scheduler waiting, so no real-time bound is claimed.
space: O(1) algorithmic shared gate state and scalar local state per worker, excluding judge-owned thread stacks, print callback and observed output transcript.
edges: limit 0/1 and endpoints divisible by 3, 5 or both.
All 24 launch orders, delayed owning worker and consecutive ordinary values.
Wrong printing role, duplicate/omitted output and overlapping calls are invalid.
Independent repeated cases must not inherit permits or static counters.

description: Implement deadlock-free dining philosophers with real competing workers and exclusive adjacent fork locks. Philosophers 0..philosophers-1 sit in a ring; philosopher p needs forks p and (p+1)%philosophers simultaneously to eat. Implement Dine(role,philosophers,bites,context), called once by each worker, so every philosopher finishes exactly bites eating operations and releases both forks before returning. Any safe eating order is accepted.
constraints: philosophers is 2..6 and bites is 0..4. Each philosopher runs in its own real native thread (Node worker_threads for JavaScript). Forks 0..philosophers-1 start unheld. All workers start independently, with varied launch order and entry delays. No philosopher may eat without both of its own adjacent forks, use a fork held by another philosopher, or return holding a fork.

context.Take(fork) blocks until the specified exclusive fork lock is acquired; context.Drop(fork) releases a fork held by the current worker. Only the two adjacent fork indices for that role are allowed. context.Eat() performs that worker actual eating operation and may take time before returning; it is valid only while both adjacent forks are held. Exactly bites Eat calls per role are required. All context objects are opaque and bound to their own worker; do not inspect or mutate their internals.

Use the supplied blocking fork API; no extra threads, guessed sleeps, polling, or extra synchronization resources. Each worker may make at most 10000*(bites+1) total Take/Drop/Eat calls. Invalid fork indices, dropping an unheld fork, extra/missing eating calls and noncompletion fail. Zero bites requires no eating and permits immediate return.

JSON fixtures contain philosophers, bites, a permutation launchOrder of all role indices, a scheduling delayMask in 0..2^philosophers-1, and [] for the context. The callable receives role, philosophers, bites and its provided context, not the scheduling arrays. Cases own independent forks and worker state.

The displayed result is a private transcript of roles calling Eat, not your return value. Its length is philosophers*bites and each role appears exactly bites times; any safe interleaving is accepted. A concrete example gives one possible transcript, not a required scheduling order. Return void/None/undefined. Assume runnable workers are eventually scheduled; no real-time fairness bound is required.
why: If every philosopher takes a differently named left fork first, a circular wait is possible. Numbering the physical forks gives every worker one common order: acquire the lower-numbered needed fork, then the higher-numbered one. A waiting chain must then move strictly toward larger fork numbers, which cannot form a cycle. Hold both through Eat, then release both; independent nonadjacent philosophers may still eat concurrently.
correctness: Every successful iteration acquires both distinct adjacent forks through exclusive locks before Eat, and releases each afterward, so mutual exclusion and per-philosopher fork requirements hold. When a worker blocks holding one fork, it holds the lower and waits for the higher. A circular wait would require strictly increasing fork numbers around a cycle, impossible in a finite ordered set. Thus deadlock cannot occur. Under eventual scheduling, a worker at the end of any waiting chain completes its finite Eat and releases forks; repeated progress with finitely many requested iterations lets every worker finish. The loop calls Eat exactly bites times for its own role and zero times when bites=0. Release order does not affect the increasing acquisition invariant.
walkthrough: For three philosophers and one bite each, role 0 needs forks 0 and 1; role 1 needs 1 and 2; role 2 needs 2 and 0. All use increasing physical order, so role 2 takes 0 before 2. One possible schedule lets role 0 take 0/1, eat and release; then role 1 takes 1/2 and eats; then role 2 takes 0/2 and eats. The observed transcript [0,1,2] is valid, but [2,1,0] or another safe order is also accepted. With four philosophers, roles 0 and 2 may eat concurrently because their fork pairs are disjoint.
time: O(bites) fixed synchronization/eating calls per worker, O(philosophers*bites) total algorithmic calls. Blocking/scheduler waiting and opaque eating duration are excluded; no fixed elapsed-time or starvation-latency bound is claimed.
space: O(philosophers) shared fork-lock state provided by the judge, O(1) local algorithm storage per worker, excluding native thread stacks and private observed transcript.
edges: Two philosophers need the same pair of distinct forks.
Zero bites and repeated independent cases.
Wraparound role must order forks 0 and philosophers-1 by physical number.
Only adjacent fork ownership permits eating; all locks must be released at return.
Different eating/release orders remain valid if safety and completion hold.
related: The primary QuestionB orders Chopstick objects by their physical numbers to break circular wait. QuestionA uses try-lock attempts that may give up without eating; this explicitly stated blocking-API variant requires every requested bite to complete and does not count failed attempts as meals.

title: Dining Philosophers

csharp.signature: void Dine(int role, int philosophers, int bites, ForkContext context)

python.signature: def Dine(role: int, philosophers: int, bites: int, context: ForkContext) -> None
python.starterCode:
def Dine(role: int, philosophers: int, bites: int, context: ForkContext) -> None:
    return
python.solutionCode:
def Dine(role: int, philosophers: int, bites: int, context: ForkContext) -> None:
    left, right = role, (role + 1) % philosophers
    lower, higher = min(left, right), max(left, right)
    for _ in range(bites):
        context.Take(lower)
        context.Take(higher)
        context.Eat()
        context.Drop(higher)
        context.Drop(lower)

description: Implement a deadlock-preventing lock factory. Owners declare the order in which they intend to acquire resource locks. Admit a declaration exactly when replacing that owner previous order leaves the union resource-dependency graph acyclic. Then grant locks only in each owner accepted order. Return the exact native lock from the provided pool, not a resource number, boolean or newly created independent lock.
constraints: Construct DeadlockFreeLocks(resourceCount,pool), where resourceCount is 1..6 and the supplied LockPool has one stable ResourceLock per resource index 0..resourceCount-1. pool.Get(resource) returns that same borrowed lock object each time. Each ResourceLock exposes Lock()/Unlock() for actual exclusive native locking. The factory must not acquire/release locks during construction, Declare or GetLock, and must not delete or replace pool-owned locks.

Owners are signed integer IDs, with supported IDs 0..3. Declare(owner,order) returns a boolean. Invalid owner/resource indices or duplicate resource IDs return false atomically. An empty order is valid. For a valid candidate, form directed edges between consecutive resources in every active owner order, replacing only the candidate owner previous order. Return true and store a copy only if that graph is acyclic; otherwise return false and preserve every prior accepted order and next-request position. A successfully replaced order resets that owner next-request position to its beginning.

All Declare calls occur before GetLock calls. These administration calls are serialized; this interface does not require concurrent mutation of factory bookkeeping. The caller may mutate its order array after Declare returns: stored dependencies and pending order must remain unchanged. Declare itself preserves the caller array. Different factory instances own independent declaration/progress state, even when they borrow the same pool.

GetLock(owner,resource) returns the exact pool.Get(resource) object only when resource is the next not-yet-granted resource in that owner accepted order; advance only then. Unknown/invalid owners, wrong/out-of-bounds resource, no declaration, empty/exhausted order or out-of-order requests return null/None/nullptr without consuming a pending resource. Lookup does not acquire the returned lock.

Clients must acquire granted locks in the order received, hold them until their work finishes, and then release them. The deadlock-prevention guarantee applies to this protocol; direct rogue pool access or out-of-order acquisition is not covered. The judge executes real competing native clients on granted orders and checks exclusive lock identity/ownership and completion. JavaScript marshals the checked stable lock identities to shared native worker mutexes; it does not run a sequential graph-only substitute.

JSON fixtures contain resourceCount, up to 20 declaration rows [owner,...orderedResources], up to 40 request pairs [owner,resource], and [] for the injected pool. Each row/resource/owner member is a signed 32-bit integer. The callable is the full factory class, not a function returning a transcript. Private display is {"declarations":[admission booleans],"grants":[whether each GetLock returned a native lock]}; it is an observation, not the class return value.
why: A resource-dependency edge means an owner can hold one lock before requesting the next. A directed cycle permits circular waiting, so admit only an acyclic combined dependency graph. Build each candidate graph from the complete active per-owner orders before committing: deleting candidate edges on rejection can accidentally remove an edge still needed by another owner. Keep per-owner request positions separately so an invalid lookup never silently skips a required acquisition.
correctness: Initially every owner order is empty and the graph has no edges. For Declare, validate bounds/distinctness before indexing. Rebuild the candidate union using the new path only for the target owner, and compute reachability by Floyd-Warshall. After processing intermediate vertices through k, reach[i][j] exactly describes paths whose internal vertices are among those processed; induction over k establishes complete reachability. A true diagonal entry is exactly a directed cycle, so rejection and admission follow the stated graph policy. No live state changes until admission; cloning the order and resetting only its cursor preserves other owners and caller independence. GetLock compares only the next pending resource and advances exactly on a match, returning the stable provided identity. Thus clients following granted orders obey the admitted resource DAG. A circular wait would imply a resource-dependency cycle, impossible in that DAG; finite clients under eventual scheduling complete and release their locks.
walkthrough: With 3 resources, owner 0 declares [0,1] (accept), owner 1 declares [1,2] (accept), and owner 2 declares [2,0] (reject: 0→1→2→0 would be cyclic). GetLock(0,1) returns null and leaves 0 pending. GetLock(0,0) then GetLock(0,1) return the actual locks 0 and 1. Owner 1 can obtain 1 then 2; owner 2 has no accepted order. After owner 0 is exhausted, another GetLock(0,1) returns null. The native clients may contend on lock 1, but no circular wait exists.
time: Declare takes O(R^3 + sum(active order lengths) + new order length), dominated by O(R^3) for R resources and four owners with distinct-resource paths. GetLock takes O(1) bookkeeping plus the provided constant-time pool lookup. Native client acquisition waiting is outside these administration-method costs.
space: O(sum(active order lengths)+4) persistent factory state and O(R^2) temporary reachability/seen storage per Declare, excluding the borrowed native lock pool and client threads. Returned locks are borrowed identities, not copies or owned allocations.
edges: Empty order, invalid signed indices, repeated resources and exhausted lookups.
Atomic rejection, shared edges belonging to several owners and replacement that removes only one owner old dependencies.
Out-of-order GetLock must not consume the next resource.
Caller changes its old array; independent factory instances share a pool without sharing orders.
Acyclic nonnumeric resource orders are valid; no global ascending-order restriction is imposed.
related: The primary LockFactory establishes upfront declaration, cycle admission and enforcing declared acquisition order. This independent class makes empty orders, owner replacement, rollback/shared-edge preservation, input ownership and the client protocol explicit. It supplies stable native locks rather than replacing the task with a cycle-detection boolean.
